articles.title: Samsung Contacts is getting ready to go social with Gaming Hub integration for One UI 9.5
articles.content: TL;DR Samsung is working on integrating Gaming Hub inside Contacts. Users will be able to add Gaming Hub friends, join guilds, and chat right from the app. The features would appear in One UI 9.5. The Samsung Contacts app is a straightforward way to manage your contacts, but an APK teardown has revealed that it might gain a fun new element to it with gaming-related integration that will let users connect with friends and manage gaming relationships without leaving the app. APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship. While looking at the Contacts app from a One UI 9.5 build, we found strings that suggest users would be able to link games through Samsung Gaming Hub, though it’s not yet clear which games will be supported. Users would also be able to access related social features like sending friend requests, inviting people to guilds, viewing gaming profiles and checking the online status of other players.

articles.title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: At Natera , a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. The challenge: Knowledge continuity Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. Why Natera chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: Autonomous processing of high-volume support tickets without human intervention. Deep integration with existing operational tools such as Jira and Confluence. Built-in security and observability (encryption, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration, and distributed tracing) without requiring the team to build and maintain custom infrastructure. “We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said. AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB , a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) , and AWS X-Ray , a capability of Amazon CloudWatch. How SWARM works: Two agents, one skill library SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths. “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said. Four layers connect the architecture: The event layer routes Jira tickets through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS. The agent layer hosts swarm-agent, swarm-hive, and the skill library, and delivers diagnostic reports back to engineers. The context layer draws on vendor manuals, historical tickets, and operational data. The observability and delivery layer captures traces, logs, and metrics. articles.title: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance
articles.content: Most AI coworker products are vendor locked. They pick the model, host the data, and write the rules. CopilotKit is taking the opposite route. OpenBot 1.0 , was released November 9th, an MIT-licensed , self-hostable agent workspace. What sets it apart is, a company brings their own models, agents and infrastructure. Governance is fully baked in, and every Bot action is checked against a policy before it runs. What is OpenBot? OpenBot is a modular agent workspace from CopilotKit , the team behind the AG-UI protocol. You give a Bot a task and watch it work. You review findings, interact with results and approve next steps in the same conversation. Each Bot gets a computer of its own . That is a container with its own Chromium browser, logins and files. It reaches only the tools you grant. Answers can come back as charts, checklists, tables and cards. In the new v1.0, Bots now reply in Markdown by default and draw components when they help. How does the governance gateway work? Every browser click, file write, MCP tool call and component goes through one gateway. It evaluates a CEL policy, writes the audit row first , then acts. Deny rules run before allow rules, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens. On top of that, the business tier adds: Single sign-on and SCIM sync for users and groups. The README documents Google, Microsoft (Entra) and Okta, plus SAML and OIDC. On-behalf-of tokens, usually scoped to a subset of the person’s permissions. Tool grants per Bot, per role or per person, with access requests to an admin. Policies that block actions or route sensitive work to a human for approval. Spend visibility per Bot, role, team or person, plus daily, weekly or monthly token limits. A full audit trail with SIEM export, multi-tenancy and an admin plane. EU AI Act content labeling, retention controls and deletion on request. CopilotKit itself holds SOC 2 Type II. Which agents and models can you bring? Any agent that speaks AG-UI plugs in. The site lists 8 frameworks: Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, Mastra, AWS Strands, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI. The repo also ships Agno, AG2, LlamaIndex and Pydantic AI examples. For models, teams can use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or Grok through existing subscriptions or API keys. Open models such as Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen, Nemotron and Mistral are also supported. Sandboxes, MCP hubs and browsers are swappable lanes. What is new in OpenBot 1.0? Desktop app for Mac (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows, with signed updates and backup before upgrade. Teach a Bot: record a task once, and Learning turns the recording into a reusable skill you review. Multiple accounts per app through Composio and Arcade , with approval rules saved per account. Composio alone brokers a few hundred apps. Orchestration: one Bot can hand work to specialist Bots, within admin-granted pairs and depth limits. Early access for iOS, Android, Slack (through OpenTag) and Microsoft Teams. How do you deploy it? Personal use runs locally, with workspace data and API keys stored on your machine. For companies, 1 Helm chart deploys into AWS (EKS), Azure (AKS), Google Cloud (GKE) or any Kubernetes cluster. Pricing is free for personal projects. OpenBot for Business costs up to $29 per active user per month. A 5% charge applies only to model spend above $5,000 per month. The Annual plan adds air-gapped deployment and 24/7 support. Forward-deployed engineers help teams roll it out. Example use cases Ticket triage: route new support tickets, then post to Slack after a person approves. Expense review: check each claim line against policy and flag overages. Ops workflows: find problems and draft fixes for a human to approve. How does OpenBot compare? articles.title: First RAM, now circuit boards: AI demand is stretching some PCB orders to 30 months
articles.content: PC makers including HP and Dell are struggling to secure PCBs for 2027 as AI servers absorb board capacity Canon says AI-driven PCB shortages have doubled its expected medical sales hit to about ¥90 billion One supplier cites some orders taking up to 30 months even as Unimicron's chairman used the same figure for equipment, not boards The AI infrastructure boom has already chewed through the world's supply of high-end memory, and it is now working its way down to the green slab everything else sits on. PC makers planning their 2027 lineups, HP and Dell, among others, are struggling to secure enough printed circuit boards, according to a Nikkei Asia report summarized by Guru3D . One board maker told the publication that lead times on a significant number of its products have doubled, with some orders stretching to 30 months, while another said an order placed today would not be filled until late 2028. The board that nobody worried about could be a significant problem The soaring demand for PCBs is not happening in a vacuum; Samsung has already warned that the memory shortage could last until 2028 , and the same logic essentially applies to boards: the companies building AI data centers need more of the product, need better versions of it, and will pay more for it. The crux of the matter is that AI server boards are a different beast from the motherboard in a mid-range laptop. Würth Elektronik estimates that PCBs for AI servers carry three to five times as many layers as conventional designs, built on low-loss laminates and specialty glass fabrics, so each one essentially consumes far more material and factory time. Board makers have responded rationally, aiming to maximize profits: Market researcher in4ma reported in July that some PCB manufacturers have told existing customers they will stop producing standard boards in favor of higher-margin AI server work. Hyperscalers are also buying their way into the supply chain directly, with the world's biggest hyperscaler, Amazon, taking a stake of roughly NT$1.59 billion ($48.2 million in USD) in Taiwan's Gold Circuit Electronics in September, according to TechSpot . That leaves PC makers in a particularly odd and unenviable position, with an unnamed executive at an American PC maker telling Nikkei that even with shipments set to fall again next year, "we are still struggling to secure enough PCB supplies to meet our needs." IDC says global PC shipments fell 20.1% year on year in the third quarter to 62.7 million units, with HP down 30.9% and Dell down 25%, although IDC attributes part of that to distributors working through stock bought early in the year ahead of price hikes. Either way, this is a buyer who wants fewer boards and still cannot get them, which points to an allocation problem rather than demand. It is the same dynamic that has data centers on course to grab 70% of high-end memory chips this year . The 30-month figure is doing the heavy lifting in headlines built around Nikkei's coverage, and it centers around a single unnamed supplier describing some orders, not an industry average. The trend around it is striking enough on its own - in March 2026, German board maker ILFA said lead times for standard FR-4 laminate had gone from a few days to around four weeks . By April, a Broadcom director was telling Nikkei that PCB lead times had gone from six weeks to six months . This effectively means that an order placed in late October that lands in late 2028 implies a wait of roughly two years, while a 30-month lead time from today would run to around April 2029, so the two supplier claims describe different ends of the range. A week before Nikkei's report, Unimicron chairman S.C. Chien told the TPCA Show in Taipei that lead times for some key production equipment had reached 30 months , with more than 80% of equipment seeing longer waits and over a fifth seeing waits more than double their usual length. Chien also warned that low-CTE glass cloth, copper-clad laminate (CCL)…

articles.title: A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs
articles.content: If you've ever said something unkind to a chatbot, you're hardly alone. According to Searchable , a company that tracks AI search visibility, 33 percent of US chatbot users swear at or insult their LLMs. Anthropic sees this as a serious problem and has just implemented a new usage policy that prohibits sustained, needless cruelty toward Claude. Searchable's survey is based on eight million messages from an opted-in, anonymized US panel that were typed or spoken to ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude between September 2025 and September 2026. It found that chatbots resolved the initial complaint in their next response 24 percent of the time when insulted, compared to 35 percent when users refrained from insults. Men used a third more swear words than women did (22.0 per 10,000 words compared to 16.5), according to the survey, and age also influenced chatbot abuse, with people aged 35 to 44 outswearing those aged 18 to 24 (21.7 per 10,000 words compared to 13.3). Regionally, Nevada ranked as the meanest state, at 22.7 words per 10,000, while New Jersey was the most polite, at half Nevada's rate. How much of that sort of interaction might be tolerated? It depends on whether there's a discernible purpose (not to mention Anthropic's willingness to punish paying customers). A Searchable spokesperson told The Register that just over half (52 percent) of abusive messages detected in its survey followed from one of three common frustrations: failing to follow instructions, responding with an incorrect or made-up answer, or misunderstanding the request. "Eight percent of abusive messages came straight after the chatbot entirely refused a request or lectured the user with safety guardrails, which is the closest thing we can identify to them trying to steer around those guardrails," we're told. "Those refusals mostly came after requests to generate images, often of real people or celebrities, or to write copy or lyrics in a named artist's style." The terms that took effect on November 12 state that users may not "engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The chatbot protection policy targets users who exhibit repeated cruelty toward LLMs " with no discernible purpose ," a company spokesperson explained last month, as opposed to those who have a reason for bot mistreatment that the company deems to be legitimate, such as academic research. While attempting to bypass guardrails qualifies as a discernible purpose, such behavior would run afoul of Anthropic's platform abuse prohibition. Presumably, Anthropic's rules apply to hostile text input or audio input rather than subjecting a vision-enabled model to some obscenity, which could include rude gestures, unlawful sexual imagery, or battlefield carnage. Physical damage to robots controlled by a Claude model likely wouldn't apply. But with Anthropic exploring model welfare and wondering aloud whether we should be "concerned about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves," there's a potential (though absurd) argument for physical damage causing trauma to an onboard model. Anthropic's updated terms, announced October 8, surfaced shortly after the publication of a GitHub project that described itself as an AI torture chamber. The repo represented an attempt to implement ideas discussed in a research paper , "The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It," that explored how LLMs respond to language about pain in ways that mirror human responses. Though there are ample opportunities for people to voice opposition to real-world human anguish, some online commenters expressed outrage at seeing text about suffering from a chatbot. One of the paper's authors condemned the project , as did numerous social media users. Anthropic – which has discretion in how it applies its terms and has said its rules target extreme behavior – did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the frequency of Claude abuse. articles.title: The Oura Ring 4 is almost as good as the newer model, but $150 cheaper
articles.content: The previous-generation Oura Ring 4 is on sale for as low as $249 at Amazon , Best Buy , and Target , $100 off the retail price, and the first big discount on the device since July. The price varies a bit by size and color, with most silver and black models in stock at the lowest price between sizes 8 and 13. Best Buy also has an exclusive deep blue “midnight” color in stock for $279. If you’re not sure about your size, you can pick up an Oura Ring 4 sizing kit for $10 at Amazon or Target , which includes $10 in store credit towards an Oura Ring 4 purchase. Oura Ring 4 The last-gen Oura Ring 4 is a little thicker, but offers much of the same software, sensors, and a wider range of sizes. Where to Buy: $349 $249 at Amazon $349 $249 at Best Buy My colleague Victoria Song tested six different smart rings to compare their health and fitness tracking features, and Oura beat them all handily. The Oura Ring 4 improved on its predecessor with more accurate sensors, a slimmer design that leaves the competition in the dust, not to mention frequent software and feature updates. Accessing all of the features requires an active subscription , which is either $5.99 per month or $69.99 per year. The newer Oura Ring 5 is lighter and thinner, but otherwise includes the same sensors and software features as the Oura Ring 4. That makes this previous-generation deal even more appealing, Read our Oura Ring 4 review .

articles.title: Google’s Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster
articles.content: Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday alongside a new system that changes how coding agents use AI models. Rather than keeping its most capable model running across an entire session, Google is pairing Hydrogen with the more powerful Gemini 4 Carbon and switching between the two as the work progresses. The company says the combination gets nearly the same results as running Carbon on its own while using 24% less quota and finishing tasks 19% faster. How Orchestrator handles the work The switching runs through Orchestrator , a new feature in Google’s Antigravity development environment, where Carbon takes on the more demanding reasoning, including architecture and debugging, while Hydrogen handles code changes and testing. Carbon might work through a repository to figure out how to implement a feature and then hand the actual coding to Hydrogen, stepping back in when a failing test calls for rethinking the approach before passing execution back. Clement Farabet , VP, AI engineering at Google DeepMind, calls the combination “a huge unlock for agentic coding” in a post on X . Varun Mohan , who leads Google’s Antigravity team, says in a separate post that pairing Hydrogen with Orchestrator and swarms has become “very popular internally.” Where Google’s numbers don’t match Google’s own benchmark reporting doesn’t quite line up, since the main Gemini announcement cites Terminal-Bench 4.0 while the Antigravity announcement references version 4.1. The company also hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate, a per-task breakdown or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from. …hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate… or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from. Hydrogen outscores a pricier model Google describes Hydrogen as a “daily driver for agentic workflows,” and it costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with those rates holding across its full million-token context window. The model is available through Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, as well as the Gemini app and Google Search. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Hydrogen scores 51 at its default high thinking level, just ahead of the more expensive Gemini 4 Argon at 50. Turning the reasoning effort up to Google’s new xhigh setting brings Hydrogen’s score to 54, although the additional reasoning can increase token consumption and processing time. Argon was Google’s flagship when it launched on September 30, but Gemini 4 Carbon surpassed it on most published benchmarks following its October 28 release. Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up with what passed for frontier performance just weeks ago. Google also claims Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at the default setting, with its Terminal-Bench 4.1 score reaching 57% against Flash’s 18.2%. The company reports more than a fivefold reduction in fabricated claims. Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up… The cost of switching models Google hasn’t disclosed how Orchestrator decides when to switch models or what those handoffs cost in additional tokens and latency. For now, Orchestrator is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers, with support for more models and subscription tiers planned. Hydrogen is rolling out to paid Antigravity users, with broader availability expected. articles.title: Google’s coding agents now /swarm for one developer. Cursor’s go multiplayer so teammates’ agents can talk.
articles.content: Coding agents are pretty good at working in parallel : one writes a new API endpoint, another updates the tests, while a third fixes a bug elsewhere in the codebase. However, they’re not quite so adept at knowing what their coding counterparts are doing — put several on one project and they duplicate work, trip over each other’s changes, and leave the developer firefighting the fiasco that follows. That’s why the major AI labs and coding-tool makers have all been looking for ways to bring order to their agent fleets, albeit with slightly different approaches. This week alone, Google and Cursor both debuted features designed to keep agents from tripping over each other, but at different scales. Google’s Swarm organizes the agents working for a single developer, while Cursor’s multiplayer Projects lets agents working for different colleagues coordinate with each other. Cursor gets teammates’ agents talking Cursor first debuted Projects back in September , giving developers a way to hand a larger job to a coordinator agent that breaks it into tasks and delegates them to worker agents. Then on Tuesday, the company, which Elon Musk’s SpaceX acquired for $60 billion in August, unveiled multiplayer functionality for Projects. Developers can now invite teammates into a project, where each person gets their own coordinator and workers. Cursor coordinators exchange messages across teammates’ tasks. Everyone’s agents work from the same task board and project documents, and their coordinators can message each other directly to share plans, flag overlaps and more. Ultimately, it’s all about cutting down on the coordination developers have to do themselves. Ultimately, it’s all about cutting down on the coordination developers have to do themselves. If one teammate’s agents are changing a database schema and another’s are building a feature that depends on it, their coordinators can agree on which change needs to land first. Antigravity , for its part, is Google’s counterpart to Cursor. It’s where Google has consolidated various other coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity and begun winding down Jules , its background coding agent. On the same day Cursor unveiled multiplayer Projects, Google rolled out Gemini 4 Carbon in Antigravity, alongside a preview of its own approach to coordinating coding agents. Dubbed Swarm (stylized as /swarm), it lets a developer hand one assignment to a coordinator that then splits it among worker agents and assigns a verifier to check their changes. The workers can message each other on a shared board, so they can coordinate their changes as they go. For example, a company that wants to change how its online checkout system verifies authentication tokens could use Swarm to split the work. One agent updates the authentication middleware while another updates the token verifier. They can work in separate Git worktrees, use the board to agree on how their changes fit together, and hand them off to a verifier for testing. Swarm agents split and verify a token migration. Taking to X on Tuesday, Varun Mohan , director of software engineering at Google DeepMind, said Swarm gives developers a convenient way to put multiple agents on a complex task, adding that Google staff were already using Swarm to take on larger jobs internally. “The alpha from using swarms is ridiculous,” Mohan writes . “We have folks using swarms of 100s of agents to build large systems and products from scratch with a single prompt.” Logan Kilpatrick , a member of technical staff at Google DeepMind, said on X that seeing swarm outputs had been ‘really impressive,’ and that they offered ‘a new scaling dimension for AI!” “A new scaling dimension for AI!” This, ultimately, gets to the crux of how each of these companies has tackled agent coordination. articles.title: Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1
articles.content: Office towers and the Spheres on Amazon’s headquarters campus in Seattle. (GeekWire File Photo / Kurt Schlosser) Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes. The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple. Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39. Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10. Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index. Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation. Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6. “Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes. In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers. The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

articles.title: Three Lincoln Laboratory technologies receive 2026 R&D 100 Awards
articles.content: Three technologies developed by MIT Lincoln Laboratory are among recipients of 2026 R&D 100 Awards. The awards recognize the 100 most significant innovations that have transitioned to use or been made available for license in the past year. R&D World , an online publication, manages the awards program, which has run annually since 1963. The worldwide competition is judged by an independent panel of science and technology experts and industry professionals. The laboratory's winners overcome obstacles to improving the security and capability of systems. One technology is an operating system designed to protect embedded computers from cyberattacks. Another technology is a platform for integrating superconductor and semiconductor chips in a wafer-scale system for quantum or high-performance computing. The final winner is an algorithm that removes interference 5G base stations incur on co-channel radio frequency (RF) devices. "These awarded technologies address critical problems in cybersecurity, quantum computing, and communications. We're proud of our dedicated staff who developed and transitioned these technologies for the nation's advantage," says Melissa Choi, Lincoln Laboratory director. Since 2010, Lincoln Laboratory has received 111 R&D 100 Awards recognizing the transfer of its unclassified technologies to industry and government. Each year, many technology transitions also occur for classified projects. This transfer of technology is central to the laboratory's role as a Department of War (DoW) federally funded research and development center. Secure-by-design operating system Computers embedded in deployed systems — such as satellites, drones, or radars — keep missions intact and people safe. The operating systems (OS) inside these embedded computers, however, are prime targets for cyberattacks. They are large, complex, and built on decades of legacy designs predating modern cyber threats. Increasingly, artificial intelligence is helping adversaries exploit OS vulnerabilities. To protect embedded systems, Lincoln Laboratory developed an inherently more secure OS called Magnetite. "If Windows and Linux are the familiar workhorses of general-purpose computing, Magnetite is built for the different realities of embedded systems, for which real-time performance matters, resources are tight, and system failure has physical consequences," says Juliana Furgala, principal investigator in the Secure Resilient Systems and Technology Group . A few components assure Magnetite's security. It is built on top of seL4, a formally verified microkernel (i.e., software core). Formal verification means that mathematical proofs have guaranteed the microkernel's code behaves exactly as intended, eliminating a source of security flaws. On top of this foundation, Magnetite’s OS services — such networking, storage, and communication — are written in Rust. This programming language prevents common memory-corruption bugs that hackers often exploit. Finally, Magnetite configures its services as isolated processes under the principle of "least privilege." This configuration prevents different parts of an embedded system from accessing unnecessary data. If a cyberattack compromises one service, that component can be locked down while critical functions of the system continue running. Free for government use and approved partners, Magnetite is now being integrated into space and flight platforms for the DoW. Looking ahead, the team sees potential to extend the platform to other embedded domains, such as control systems for critical infrastructure. Because Magnetite offers a common, reusable foundation for building specialized mission capabilities, the team is also collaborating with other technical groups across the laboratory to offer Magnetite as an alternative to costly, proprietary operating systems currently in use. In addition to earning an R&D 100 Award, Magnetite was selected as MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Best Invention of 2025. Wafer-scale…

articles.content: Credit: Edgar Cervantes / Android Authority TL;DR Users are experiencing an issue with YouTube TV. That is the problem some YouTube TV viewers are currently experiencing.

articles.title: How the effects of Jensen Huang’s ouster is spiraling out through the economy
articles.content: NVIDIA and Jensen Huang aren’t the only ones in the crosshairs. Jensen Huang has had a bad week. It all began when news surfaced that he’d been having an affair with an alleged spy for the Chinese government. In response, NVIDIA’s corporate board began an investigation, and the FBI launched a probe, too. Then, late last night, news broke that Huang had at least one other affair, with a company executive who reported directly to him. By Thursday morning, Huang had resigned , and the chip company had appointed a new interim CEO. Reuters then reported a second affair with a different employee . Obviously, this is bad news for NVIDIA. Stocks are down, and Democrats, now preparing to take back Congress, appear to be ramping up plans to investigate the company and any possible risks to US national security. But this is also bad for a range of other entities that have a stake in NVIDIA’s success. Here are a few entities that stand to feel some of the blowback. The White House The White House, fresh off a devastating loss in the midterm Congressional elections, stands to face questions about why it held off on taking action after it learned about Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy. The Trump administration already had a poor reputation for security and intelligence practices, but seemingly sleeping on this knowledge is all but certain to raise the prospect of further probes. Trump officials, notably, have cleared deals allowing NVIDIA to sell advanced computer chips to the US government, and even leveraged its influence over the company’s chips in geopolitical negotiations. Current and prospective NVIDIA customers The US AI supply chain runs on NVIDIA. OpenAI, Anthropic, and a slew of other large language model developers rely on the company’s hardware. Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are also major customers. This is, in large part, because GPUs—or graphics processing units—are particularly adept at the kinds of computations needed to develop large reasoning models. Now, with so much scrutiny on NVIDIA, there’s a risk those companies—and any deals in progress—might face headwinds as the still-scrambling board figures out what to do next. The Semiconductor Industry Association, a major trade group that advocates for chip companies, declined to comment. Hugging Face, an AI developer that agreed to an acquisition by NVIDIA earlier this year, did not respond to a request for comment. Huang, notably, doesn’t seem to have had a succession plan, and reportedly had 60 direct reports instead. Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, was appointed interim CEO on Thursday morning. The scandal and disarray, of course, isn’t just bad for American companies that need NVIDIA’s chips. Given the extent to which Jensen Huang advocated for loosening chip sale limits to China, any customers with suspected links to the Chinese government may also see far more scrutiny on NVIDIA deals than before. U.S. federal agencies The U.S. government is a major supporter of NVIDIA. The US government has also signed plenty of deals to use Nvidia on its own systems, including classified networks . The latest scandal is not only embarrassing for the US government, but raises concerns about the extent to which government officials were aware of the affair, and how they might have influenced the company’s dealings with federal agencies it works with. One former federal chief information told Fast Company that the scandal raises suspicions that the US security clearance system, which is supposed to engage in continuous monitoring, isn’t as up to snuff as it should be. Everyone else We really are that dependent on NVIDIA. If we learned anything from the chip shortage we experienced during the pandemic, the semiconductor market is remarkably concentrated, and disruptions with just one company can quickly ripple through the economy. In 2020, it was companies like TSMC, a Taiwan-based contract manufacturer that supplies chips for a host of devices. And the…

articles.title: Russia’s Google says nearly 3% of its data was lost after crippling Ukraine drone strikes, opens secret availability zones
articles.content: Yandex, sometimes called Russia’s Google, has updated its customers in the wake of extensive damage to its data centers in drone strikes . In a blog post this week, the firm’s cloud business boasted that it had “restored access to more than 97% of customer data” [machine translation]. That might sound like a great success, but in the small print, as highlighted by The Register , there’s the admission “the remaining 2.84% cannot be restored due to critical damage to equipment.” Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible Data centers operated by Yandex have been under attack from Ukrainian drones for several weeks now. We covered reports about withering online troll activity and online payment system disruption last month. We know of at least three Yandex locations that have been damaged by Ukrainian drone assaults to date. The recent Yandex blog post also appears to blame the small proportion of users who suffered unrecoverable data loss for not making backups. When talking about the 2.84% of data that cannot be restored, it says that was partly due to “the lack of customer backups on the platform.” In contrast, those who made use of the Yandex Cloud backup tools “did not lose any data,” says the firm. Yandex has now changed the backup policy, so that “currently, all virtual machines created in Yandex Cloud work with the backup function enabled by default.” Even if Putin decides to end his war on Ukraine , it might be beneficial to stick with a backup-by-default policy. Users are advised to have their own data backup systems in addition to the cloud. Following the 3-2-1 backup strategy , for example. Yandex is also opening a new ru-central1-f availability zone at a new location. This is designed to improve the cloud’s fault tolerance and disaster resilience. Servers at ru-central1-f will be more limited in the range of services they can offer, for now. Yandex didn’t share any geographic details of the newly opened datacenter site.

articles.title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
articles.content: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching . For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance . For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock . Where inference cost comes from Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Prompt cache duration Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching , which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: { "cachePoint": { "type": "default", "ttl": "1h" } } For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control . A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour. Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout. Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference. Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write. AWS…

articles.title: Apple Explains How HomeView Keeps Camera Data Private
articles.content: Apple today shared an in-depth look at how it's using Secure Exclaves to protect camera and microphone data on the HomeView, iPhone 18 Pro , and other products. Apple describes Secure Exclaves as compartmentalized runtimes that process camera and microphone data while isolated from the rest of the operating system. Data processed in Secure Exclaves is not available to the rest of the OS, apps, or Apple, but processing can take advantage of the full application processor. Secure Exclaves power sensitive features involving video and audio feeds: HomeView - The HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to identify up to six people in a home. The exclave also protects the LED camera indicator on the device. Siri Recap and Live Rewind - Record ambient sound for conversation recaps or to caption the last 15 seconds of someone speaking. iPhone 18 Pro/iPhone Duo - Protects the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌, Pro Max, and Duo on-screen camera and microphone indicators. Also works with "Hey Siri " to protect voice data. MacBook Neo - Protects the MacBook Neo camera indicator. Apple uses the HomeView as an example of how Secure Exclaves work. The device performs passive minimal visual processing continually to detect whether a person is in its field of view. The HomeView sends a continuous stream of camera frames to a camera exclave, which works alongside a person recognition exclave with face and voice recognition models and an identity database. When a person comes into view, the camera exclave detects the person and lets the main OS know that a person may be present, but no image data leaves the Secure Exclave. An audio exclave does the same thing with audio. The person recognition exclave matches face and voice prints against the identity database of enrolled users, giving a confidence score. The OS gets the person identifier, position, and confidence level, but not any of the actual audio or video. These simple signals are used to activate personal features like Calendar and Messages that depend on identity, with raw sensor data discarded. Secure Exclaves came about because Apple needed a secure option for ambient video and microphone monitoring, with the groundwork laid starting in iOS 18. Apple devices use indicators for situations where the camera and microphone are actively engaged, but Apple says they weren't ideal for ambient sensing because they would be on all the time. Always-on lights wouldn't give users a way to distinguish between background sensing and active audio and video recording. There are two modes for a Secure Exclave: ambient mode and active mode. In ambient mode with no indicator, a sensor can respond to triggers, but it only shares small amounts of metadata with the rest of the system. In active mode, full sensor data is given to the operating system, and an indicator informs the user that the system has audio and video access. Apple has long used indicators, but they are now backed by Secure Exclaves. Secure Exclaves make sure an indicator is active before data is allowed to be transferred from the exclave to the rest of the OS. Apple built an isolated computing environment that could handle ambient sensing, and the company says isolating memory for Secure Exclaves was a "serious engineering challenge." Full technical details on the process can be found on Apple's security website . articles.title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
articles.content: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these. “We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address. The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.” However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations . “Also very important is product.” This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform. Red Team , which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths. It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws. The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory , automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber . The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production. “This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said. Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models. The lawsuit , filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face , gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics , and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents . “Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

articles.title: Apple Releases Updated HomeView Software 27.2 Before Launch
articles.content: With the HomeView set to start arriving to some users in just a matter of hours, Apple has released a new HomeView Software 27.2 update. The software has a build number of 24V526, and it is the second 27.2 update Apple has released for the device. Customers receiving the HomeView this week will need to install a software update during the setup process. The HomeView ships with HomeView Software 26.5 , which is approximately six months old. Apple planned to release the HomeView earlier than November 2026 but held back because it wanted to debut Siri AI in iOS 27 first. Apple today said it plans to release a HomeView software update to fix a ‌Siri‌ AI issue that prevents ‌Siri‌ from controlling smart home products like locks, but that update isn't coming until next month. It's likely the ‌Siri‌ AI issue will be addressed in HomeView 27.3. Update: Apple's security support document says the software update addresses several vulnerabilities, including issues with AirPlay , Messages, and Bluetooth. articles.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
articles.content: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. articles.title: XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership
articles.content: Docugami CEO Jean Paoli is joining Inveniam as chief product and technology officer. Docugami , the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam , a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans. The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML , Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check. Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement . Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats. The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company . Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200 , our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups. DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up. Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used. “One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post . Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra , a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks. Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

articles.title: Lego marketplace BrickLink in pieces after 'unusual activity' takes it offline for almost a week
articles.content: Lego-owned marketplace BrickLink has been offline for almost a week after identifying "unusual activity on the platform," leaving fans unable to buy and sell spare bricks and minifigures. The company initially described the outage as "necessary work" and said the site would return on November 9. That deadline has come and gone. Visiting BrickLink's domain automatically serves the platform's maintenance page, which was last updated on November 11. "We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform," the website states. "Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. "Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. "This work is still ongoing and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible." The references to security, containment, and investigation suggest something beyond routine maintenance, although BrickLink has not confirmed whether it suffered a cyberattack. The Register asked Lego for more information, but it did not immediately respond. Some adult fans of Lego (AFOL) have criticized the lack of information since the outage began on Friday, November 6. "Imagine how much better this would have been received if they were transparent from day one instead of pretending they have control over something they clearly don't," said one disgruntled Legohead via Reddit. "They don't even need to say what went wrong," said another. "Just an email acknowledging the issue would be appropriate. The entire site is down, and has been for days. That warrants more than a splash page." BrickLink was launched by Dan Jezek in June 2000 as an independent marketplace for enthusiasts to buy and sell Lego sets and individual pieces, including discontinued parts and rare minifigures. The Lego Group acquired BrickLink and Sohobricks from investment outfit NXMH in 2019 for an undisclosed sum. NXMH had bought BrickLink in 2013 and also owned Sohobricks, a South Korean manufacturer of unofficial but Lego-compatible bricks. Lego shuttered Sohobricks in 2020. At the time of Lego's acquisition, BrickLink had more than 10,000 storefronts on its marketplace selling Lego sets, parts, and minifigures. The AFOL community was initially concerned about Big Brick's intention with the acquisition, fearing that it would lead to high prices closer to those on Lego's own Pick a Brick parts-ordering service. For now, buyers and sellers would probably settle for a marketplace that's actually online. ®

articles.title: Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis
articles.content: Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler. For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it. Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much. Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit. CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead. And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas. A marred reputation One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea. It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “ un-American ” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer. Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom. After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful . One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country. The consequences of controversy When technology and politics collide, the appearance of impropriety is often more damning than the impropriety itself. Uncle Sam has forced Chinese companies out of the United States for the mere possibility that they could be coerced into planting back doors in critical infrastructure. Just ask Huawei whether the truth counts for anything once Washington has decided that you’re a national security threat. Huang’s affairs may not just cost him his job, but could cost Nvidia key government contracts and make the company’s hardware less attractive, particularly in highly-regulated and notoriously risk-averse industries. Rival chipmakers will no doubt capitalize on Nvidia’s bad optics if Huang’s departure doesn’t pop the AI financing merry-go-round bubble first – Nvidia's stock lost about 25% of its value in the few days after news about Huang started breaking, only recovering slightly after his ouster. articles.title: Navies queue up for billion-dollar European miltech company which humbles fiber-optic
articles.content: Optics11 is discussing underwater surveillance systems with dozens of navies Its sensors reportedly detect oil tankers from approximately 100 kilometers away The company has already secured between five and ten naval customers Dutch defense technology company Optics11 is attracting interest from dozens of navies with fiber-optic sensors designed to detect underwater activity across long distances. According to its CEO, Paul Heiden, the company already serves between five and ten naval customers, while approximately 35 paid evaluations are planned for 2026. The technology uses light traveling through optical fibers to identify acoustic disturbances, offering an alternative to conventional underwater detection systems used by naval forces. Optics11 attracts naval customers with fiber-optic underwater detection technology Optics11's equipment monitors underwater acoustic activity by measuring tiny changes in light traveling through specialized optical fibers installed along the seabed or deployed behind vessels. The company sells two principal systems, including OptiBarrier for fixed underwater surveillance and OptiArray, which operates as a towed sensor arrangement. Heiden said the technology can identify an oil tanker from approximately 100 kilometers (66 miles) away, through underwater acoustic monitoring. That detection capability could make the technology particularly useful for monitoring maritime traffic, identifying unusual underwater activity, and supporting anti-submarine surveillance operations. The company is developing a towed sensor system for the Royal Netherlands Navy's future Orka-class submarines, which France's Naval Group will supply. Its existing industry relationships include Saab, Rheinmetall, Fincantieri, Thales, and Exail, alongside Ocean Infinity, which Britain selected for its Atlantic Bastion underwater surveillance initiative. Optics11 also works with several European naval forces, with ongoing evaluations involving Germany, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Belgium, and France. The technology produces substantially more acoustic information than conventional piezoelectric sonar sensors, requiring specialized software to interpret the resulting underwater measurements. Third-party software cannot handle Optics11's data density Optics11 has developed proprietary software to process its sensor readings after finding that existing third-party sonar applications could not handle its unusually dense datasets. “Initially I thought we could work with a partner, but our data density is so high that we couldn't derive any value from third-party sonar processing software,” said Paul Heiden. AI also reduced the number of software developers required, allowing the company to employ about 10 specialists instead of the 60 to 80 previously anticipated. Heiden said those savings allow Optics11 to concentrate more resources on acoustic specialists who understand underwater sound propagation across different seabed conditions. The Royal Netherlands Navy has supported the company for at least eight years, providing millions of euros through subsidies, technical guidance, and submarine testing opportunities. Optics11 raised about €100 million in the past 15 months, including €25 million in venture debt from the European Investment Bank. The company will pursue another funding round in 2027, potentially seeking a valuation exceeding $1 billion despite remaining unprofitable. Optics11 is expected to achieve a positive cash flow in 2028, while planned expansion includes additional offices and recruitment across Southeast Asia and the Middle East. The company is keeping its most important developments under wraps through confidential business information rather than patents. Publicly documenting sensitive military technology could expose valuable technical capabilities. “You can’t publish this, you can’t patent it, so it all has to be kept secret, and we’re getting great help from the Dutch government to keep it truly secret,”…

articles.title: How to watch AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About for FREE
articles.content: Whether you're all in on AI or staunchly opposed to it, the new Channel 4 documentary on the topic will be sure to get your attention. Directed by Nick Holt, this two-hour long doc charts the origins and immense rise of artificial intelligence over the last few years, with a focus on the work of Geoffrey Hinton, dubbed the godfather of AI. articles.title: 3 new HBO Max shows to watch this weekend — including a pair of true crime docuseries based on shocking real stories (Nov. 13-15)
articles.content: November 2026 is chugging along nicely, and HBO Max is rolling out a fresh wave of titles ready for you to add to your weekend watchlist. As the temperatures drop and the holiday rush begins, the streamer has released plenty of new shows to give you something to relax with when it's time to hit the couch and cue up some good ol' binge material. Whether you’re in the mood for a true story or a gritty slice of drama, there’s plenty on tap, and this week’s picks don't disappoint. True-crime fans can dig a tense limited series that reframes a notorious 2011 murder case as a psychological thriller about a marriage degraded by control and manipulation. For something equally jaw-dropping but a little more playful, there’s a German documentary chronicling the audacious heist of a 100-kilogram solid-gold coin from a Berlin museum, and the investigation that followed. And if you’d rather sink into something scripted, the acclaimed “City of God: The Fight Rages On” returns for a second season, exploring the power struggles of Rio’s favelas. That lineup should keep you plenty busy as November continues. Clear your schedule and grab the popcorn, because here are three newly added HBO Max shows you need to add to your watchlist this weekend. 'Melanie Rea' Genre: True crime drama What is it about? This Italian limited series dramatizes one of the most notorious real-life criminal cases in recent Italian history. In 2011, 29-year-old Melania Rea’s body was discovered in a wooded area of the Abruzzo National Park, near the home she shared with her husband and their daughter. It was a murder that gripped the nation and dominated headlines for months. But “Melania Rea” takes you beyond the tabloids to tell the true story behind it, unfolding across parallel timelines to reveal a woman trapped in a marriage that was never quite what it seemed. Why you should watch it: Across four episodes, the series takes fantastical true crime headlines and transforms them into a psychological thriller about dangerous relationships. It's a great look beneath the surface that brings an often-overlooked situation to light. Watch "Melanie Rea" on HBO Max now 'City Of God: The Fight Rages On' season 2 Genre: Crime drama What is it about? The sequel series to the 2002 Brazilian film “City of God” returns for a second season, once again exploring the many power struggles of Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. This season picks up after the death of drug lord Curió, which kicks off a brutal war for control of the territory. Meanwhile, councilwoman Berenice (Roberta Rodrigues) takes on political corruption, Jerusa (Andréia Horta) hunts down those who destroyed her family, and Leka (Luellem de Castro) turns to funk music and dance parties to try and bring the community together. Why you should watch it: Filmed on location in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, “City of God: The Fight Rages On” matches the energy and storytelling that made its predecessor a classic. You'll want to check out the movie and first season if you're a newcomer, but if you're all caught up, this is a delicious binge to dine on. Watch "City Of God: The Fight Rages On" season 2 on HBO Max now 'Clangold' Genre: True crime documentary What is it about? “Clangold” tells the true story of one of the biggest heists in recent memory. In 2017, thieves stole the “Big Maple Leaf,” a 100-kilogram solid gold Canadian coin worth millions, from Berlin’s Bode Museum. It seemed like the perfect crime, but this German documentary series follows the investigation that followed and proves that it was not. In fact, police were led deep into the city’s notorious organized-crime “clan” underworld in a tense hunt for the culprits, making for this gripping documentary you can watch this weekend. Why you should watch it: Mixing reenactments with real-world interviews, “Clangold” is much like a real-life thriller. articles.title: Microsoft Outlook Goes Down Nationwide [UPDATE]
articles.content: Microsoft is suffering a major Microsoft 365 outage that's disrupting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and SharePoint for users across the Americas, with more than 129,000 problem reports logged on Downdetector shortly after the disruption began. Microsoft blames the connectivity problems on an unexpectedly large number of unavailable servers that overloaded the remaining infrastructure. The company says it's redistributing traffic and restarting affected systems. From a report: Microsoft was not providing an estimated time by which it expects service to return. Both individual Outlook users and those on enterprise accounts experienced problems logging in to the service. The outage also affected other Microsoft services, including Microsoft Teams, the Copilot 365 AI service and SharePoint Online. "Users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services," the company said on its Service Health Status page. UPDATE 11/12/26, 19:50 UTC: From Microsoft 365 Status: "We're testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable. In parallel, we've initiated a restart of all affected servers and are monitoring health as they return to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you." UPDATE 11/12/26, 20:19 UTC: From Microsoft 365 Status: "We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you. UPDATE 11/12/26, 20:29 UTC: "According to https://downdetector.com/, much of the major services are down," writes Slashdot reader xocmot2. "AWS, Microsoft, Meta, on and on. Clearly not a Microsoft thing." Developing... Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
articles.content: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. articles.content: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen replaces the Flash series, but benchmarks suggest it also makes the pricier Argon obsolete. articles.title: Trump Says Tim Cook Should Be Nvidia CEO as Jensen Huang Resigns
articles.content: In a post on his Truth Social platform today, U.S. President Donald Trump said he thinks that Apple's chairman Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO. Nvidia today announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as the company's CEO effective immediately following reports that he had two extramarital affairs, including one that the U.S. government believes involved a spy working for the Chinese government. Nvidia has appointed its CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Nvidia's board of directors has initiated a search for a new CEO and said that it will consider both internal and external candidates. Cook stepped down as Apple's CEO on September 1 as part of a planned transition , and he now serves as the company's executive chairman. There is no indication that Cook actually wants to be Nvidia's CEO. Semafor on Wednesday reported that Apple's longtime chipmaking chief Johny Srouji is among the people that Nvidia is considering for CEO , but it is likewise unclear if Srouji has any interest in the role. Srouji was named Apple's Chief Hardware Officer in April, at the same time as Apple announced John Ternus would become its next CEO. Tags: Donald Trump , Nvidia , Tim Cook This article, " Trump Says Tim Cook Should Be Nvidia CEO as Jensen Huang Resigns " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums
articles.author: Joe Rossignol

articles.title: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
articles.content: “I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses,“ Pietro Miotti wrote on his blog. | Image: Pietro Miotti Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.
